course.title: AP World History: Modern
course.description: Understand the people, ideas, and connections that shaped the world from c. 1200 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Explore how states rose, belief systems spread, trade networks connected regions, and revolutions reshaped societies from c. 1200 to the present.

guide.title: Unit 1 study guide
guide.essential: How did societies build authority, organize work, and sustain shared beliefs between c. 1200 and c. 1450?

timeline.text: Background: earlier Chinese bureaucracies, Indian Ocean exchange, the rise of Islam, and older American communities shaped this period.
Southern Song China continued until 1279. The Delhi Sultanate began in 1206; Mali expanded in the thirteenth century. Baghdad fell to the Mongols in 1258.
Mansa Musa made his pilgrimage in 1324-1325. Vijayanagara emerged in 1336. Plague disrupted Eurasian societies. Ming rule began in 1368.
The Mexica Triple Alliance formed in 1428. Inca expansion accelerated under Pachacuti from about 1438. Both empires expanded further after 1450.

comparisons.caption: Regional patterns in authority, belief, and resources
rows: Song China
Examinations and appointed officials
Confucian ethics and Buddhist traditions
Agriculture, markets, taxes, and manufactures
Bureaucratic continuity alongside commercial growth.
Dar al-Islam
Multiple sultanates and dynasties
Islam, with Christian and Jewish communities
Farming, cities, commerce, and scholarly patronage
Shared practices connected politically divided territories.
South and Southeast Asia
Sultanates, regional kingdoms, and maritime states
Hinduism, Buddhism, Islam, Bhakti, and Sufism
Irrigation, land revenue, ports, and shipping
Cultural influence did not require a single regional empire.
The Americas
Maya cities, Mexica tributaries, and Inca administration
Sacred kingship and diverse local traditions
Tribute, labor obligations, intensive farming
States mobilized resources through different institutions.
Africa
Mali, Ethiopia, Great Zimbabwe, and independent cities
Islam, Christianity, and indigenous traditions
Agriculture, pastoralism, crafts, and trade
Centralized and decentralized systems coexisted.
Europe
Monarchies, nobles, city-states, and church authorities
Christianity alongside Jewish and Muslim communities
Manors, free and coerced labor, and growing markets
Regional variation complicates a single “feudal Europe” model.

pitfalls: A shared religion does not mean shared government or equal legal status.
A decentralized political system is still a political system.
Avoid projecting the peak of the Inca and Mexica empires backward to 1200.
Chinampas were constructed growing beds, not drifting islands. Terraces and raised fields were different techniques.
The Abbasid loss of Baghdad did not end Muslim scholarship everywhere.
A similar building shape is not enough to establish contact between societies.
Keep developments after 1450 labeled as later context. Do not use European conquest as a cause of thirteenth-century American changes.

topics.title: East Asia
topics.summary: Song China: an enduring government, changing economy, and influential culture.
topics.bigIdea: Song China combined long-standing ideas about authority with changes in farming and trade. Its neighbors borrowed Chinese practices while shaping societies of their own.

readingGuide.readingLabel: AMSCO Topic 1.1, supplied Unit 1 PDF pages 3-11
prompts: Trace the connection from Champa rice to specialized urban work. Include one other contributing development.
Compare the role of educated officials in Song China with warrior elites in Japan.
Use a belief or practice to show both Chinese influence and local adaptation in East Asia.

topics.title: Dar al-Islam
topics.summary: Regional Muslim states, connected communities, and the movement of ideas across Afro-Eurasia.
topics.bigIdea: Political power became divided among several Muslim states, while religion, commerce, and scholarship kept people connected across borders. A shared cultural world could survive the decline of a particular empire.

readingGuide.readingLabel: AMSCO Topic 1.2, supplied Unit 1 PDF pages 12-16
prompts: Explain one threat to Abbasid political authority and why it did not end the wider Islamic cultural world.
Choose one scholarly achievement, such as astronomy, mathematics, medicine, or historical writing, and explain its significance.
Use one example from commerce, women’s rights, religious communities, or al-Andalus to show both interaction and a limit on equality.

topics.title: South and Southeast Asia
topics.summary: Hindu, Buddhist, and Muslim communities; inland kingdoms and maritime states.
topics.bigIdea: South and Southeast Asia shared influential religious traditions, but their states drew on different combinations of land, labor, temples, and maritime commerce.

readingGuide.readingLabel: AMSCO Topic 1.3, supplied Unit 1 PDF pages 17-23
prompts: Explain one difference between the Delhi Sultanate, Rajput kingdoms, and Vijayanagara, including how the state was founded or organized.
Compare Bhakti devotion and Sufi practice without treating them as the same religion.
Explain how Khmer water infrastructure supported political authority, then contrast it with a maritime state or Sri Lankan irrigation system.

topics.title: The Americas
topics.summary: Maya cities, Mexica tribute, Inca labor, and diverse North American communities.
topics.bigIdea: American societies built cities and states using local crops, labor obligations, sacred authority, and regional exchange. Maya, Mexica, Inca, and North American communities developed distinct institutions.

readingGuide.readingLabel: AMSCO Topic 1.4, supplied Unit 1 PDF pages 27-33
prompts: Compare payments in goods with labor obligations as ways to support a state.
Explain how chinampas and Andean terraces addressed different environments.
Describe what archaeology can reveal about Cahokia or Ancestral Pueblo communities, and one limit of the evidence.

topics.title: Africa
topics.summary: African kingdoms and cities, connected by agriculture, commerce, and varied beliefs.
topics.bigIdea: African societies included large kingdoms, independent cities, and communities governed through kinship. Their rulers used agriculture, trade, religious connections, and local institutions in different combinations.

readingGuide.readingLabel: AMSCO Topic 1.5, supplied Unit 1 PDF pages 34-40
prompts: Compare Mali with the Hausa city-states on the same political dimension.
Explain how Great Zimbabwe connected an inland economy to overseas markets.
Use Ethiopia to challenge the claim that all African states adopted Islam.

topics.title: Developments in Europe
topics.summary: Religious institutions, divided political authority, and changing agricultural societies.
topics.bigIdea: European societies were largely agricultural and politically divided. Religious institutions, landholding, and labor obligations shaped authority, while growing towns and uneven political changes complicated that pattern.

readingGuide.readingLabel: AMSCO Topic 1.6, supplied Unit 1 PDF pages 41-49
prompts: Distinguish feudal relationships among elites from the manor’s labor system.
Explain one way religious institutions could support a ruler and one way they could challenge a ruler.
Trace how agricultural productivity and later population losses could change labor relationships.

topics.title: Comparisons in the Period
topics.summary: Compare authority, resources, and beliefs using precise evidence and historical reasoning.
topics.bigIdea: A strong comparison names a shared problem, supports both sides with specific evidence, and explains why the similarities or differences matter. State building followed several paths rather than a single global sequence.

readingGuide.readingLabel: AMSCO Topic 1.7, supplied Unit 1 PDF pages 50-53
prompts: Choose two states and compare the same method of maintaining authority in each.
Support one continuity and one innovation with named examples.
Revise a vague claim such as “all states were the same” into a specific, qualified comparison.
